brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: What are the two axes that form the foundation of the Social Style Selling framework?
choices: Introversion versus Extraversion, and Task versus People
Ask versus Tell, and Task versus People
Direct versus Indirect, and Emotional versus Logical
Speed versus Accuracy, and Individual versus Team
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the X axis is Ask versus Tell, and the Y axis is Task versus People.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework is built on two specific behavioral axes. The X axis focuses on how someone gets what they want (Ask or Tell), and the Y axis focuses on what drives their behavior (Task or People focus).

questions.question: Which signature question is most likely to come from a Driver?
choices: How does this work and how accurate is it?
What are the results and what is the outcome?
Why this solution and why now?
Who else is using this and who is involved?
questions.feedback_correct: Drivers lead with "What?" because they are focused on results and outcomes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a distinctive signature question. Drivers are results-focused and task-driven, so they ask "What?" to understand the outcome. The other options belong to other styles: "How?" is Analytical, "Why?" is Amiable, and "Who?" is Expressive.

questions.question: An Analytical buyer is characterized by which two behavioral traits?
choices: Animated storytelling and high emotion
Gives direction quickly and focuses on speed
Asks many questions, moves methodically, and hates being caught unprepared
Warm, soft-spoken, and avoids conflict and rushed decisions
questions.feedback_correct: Analyticals are defined by their asking nature and their methodical, data-driven approach—plus their strong aversion to being unprepared.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Analyticals are the task-focused style that asks rather than tells. They prioritize accuracy and process over speed, and they want to fully understand before moving forward. Review the Analytical profile to distinguish it from the other three styles.

questions.question: According to the course, what was the impact on sales reps who learned to read and adjust to buyer style?
choices: 72 percent improved their closing rate
58 percent closed sales they otherwise might not have closed
45 percent reduced their sales cycle
81 percent increased their commission
questions.feedback_correct: That 58 percent figure is highlighted as the key outcome—more than half of reps won business they would not have won without style awareness.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course cites specific research outcomes. While 92 percent developed better relationships and 87 percent increased influence, the 58 percent who closed additional sales is the most powerful metric for why this skill matters commercially.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of spending real time on rapport with an Amiable buyer before discussing business?
choices: To demonstrate your product knowledge and credibility
To help them feel safe and establish that relationships matter in your approach
To move the conversation quickly toward a decision
To show that you understand their budget constraints
questions.feedback_correct: Amiables need to feel safe first—rapport is not optional with this style, it is foundational to their ability to engage in business.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Amiables are people-focused and relationship-driven. Building genuine rapport before discussing business creates the safety and trust they need to move forward. Skipping this step or rushing it will cause them to withdraw.

questions.question: If a Driver buyer suddenly takes control of the meeting and becomes assertive, what does this signal according to the course?
choices: The buyer is interested and wants to accelerate the sale
A pressure behavior indicating something has broken down and you should shift your approach
The buyer is a natural leader and respects direct communication
You have successfully built rapport and can now close
questions.feedback_correct: Taking control of the meeting is a Driver's pressure behavior—a signal that something in the interaction has gone off track and needs adjustment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Pressure behaviors are not signs of strength or interest; they are warning signals that the buyer feels pushed, rushed, misunderstood, or out of control. Recognizing them early allows you to shift and recover before rapport is damaged.

questions.question: Why is it important to identify your own Social Style as a sales rep?
choices: Because some styles are naturally better at selling than others
Because your natural selling approach lands differently on buyers of different styles and may not match their needs
Because you need to change your personality for each buyer type
Because the model only works if you are a Driver or Expressive
questions.feedback_correct: Your own defaults shape how you come across, and what works for a buyer like you may shut down a buyer of a different style—that awareness is step one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Understanding your own style helps you see your blind spots. You do not need to become a different person, but you do need to recognize that your natural communication style lands differently depending on who is listening.

questions.question: A buyer is warm, emotionally open, and focused on relationships and consensus, but tends to avoid conflict and rushed decisions. Which style best describes this buyer?
choices: Driver
Analytical
Amiable
Expressive
questions.feedback_correct: This profile matches the Amiable style perfectly—people-focused, relationship-oriented, and conflict-averse.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Amiables are defined by their warmth, focus on relationships and consensus, and strong tendency to avoid conflict and pressure. While they show emotion like Expressives, Amiables ask questions rather than tell, and they prioritize harmony over visibility.

questions.question: When a buyer shows an adjacent style, what does that mean for how you should interpret their behavior?
choices: They are confused about their own preferences and you should clarify
The adjacent style softens or modifies how their primary style shows up in behavior, explaining mixed signals
You should ignore the adjacent style and focus only on the primary style
They are not being authentic and you cannot trust their responses
questions.feedback_correct: Adjacent styles sit next to the primary style on the grid and soften or shape how that primary style appears—this explains why a buyer might not be a "pure" version of their style.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Almost no one is a pure style. If a buyer seems to blend traits—like a Driver who is warmer than expected—the adjacent style is usually at work. This is not confusion or inauthenticity; it is a normal part of how Social Style works in real people.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the one core disciplined habit that defines versatility in practice?
choices: Mirroring the buyer's personality and tone in every conversation
Becoming equally skilled at all four Social Styles before meeting any buyer
Read the cues, name the style, and adjust your approach accordingly
Asking permission from the buyer before changing your communication approach
questions.feedback_correct: Versatility boils down to one repeatable habit: observe, identify, adapt—without needing to be a different person.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Versatility is not about personality transformation or becoming someone you are not. It is a disciplined, repeatable habit of reading observable cues, mentally naming the style, and consciously adjusting how you communicate to reduce friction and connect more effectively.
